newsitem.title: GREECE: Greeks to pay more for EU convergence and defence.
newsitem.headline: Greeks to pay more for EU convergence and defence.

text.p: Prime Minister Costas Simitis won a confidence vote in parliament on Sunday, calling on Greeks to tighten their belts to help the country join a single European currency and safeguard national security.
"Those who have the means will be called to contribute more," Simitis told parliament. "There is no magic way to achieve our targets without cost."

Simitis was backed by 161 deputies in the 300-seat parliament while 134 voted against him and five were absent. His socialist PASOK party scored an easy victory in elections last month which gave him an absolute majority with 162 seats.

The first unpopular measures are expected within the month with legislation that will abolish tax breaks for millions of households and a halt in public sector hirings to curb towering public deficits.
The taxing of income earned from government securities (state treasury bills and bonds) is also under consideration before the presentation of the 1997 budget at the end of November.
The target is for Greece -- the worst EU performer -- to join the European Monetary Union by the year 2000 but to achieve this, it must slash inflation and state spending with unprecedented rates.

"The distance separating our economy from the rest of the EU countries is significant. We must decide to take the step that will bring us closer," Simitis said. "Greece must participate in this effort (to meet EMU criteria) or else it will be set aside by its partners."

National Economy and Finance Minister Yannos Papandoniou said targets for 1997 included cutting the general government deficit by 3.4 percentage points and lowering the average inflation rate by two percent.
The general government deficit was expected to be 7.6 percent of GDP at the end of 1996, compared to a requirement of three percent of the GDP for participation in EMU.
Inflation was running at 8.5 percent in September, more than three times the EU average, and the EMU criteria call for an inflation rate of no more than two points above the three best EU performers.
Papandoniou said the government will carry on with a strict monetary policy that curbed inflation to a single digit at the end of 1995 for the first time after two decades of double-digit figures.

"The current foreign exchange policy is the cornerstone of our fight against inflation and can't be changed. This must be understood by the business community and markets so to adopt their behaviour," he said.
The acceleration of public and private investments would boost GDP growth by three to 3.5 percent next year compared to 2.6 percent in 1996.
Government officials expect spending cuts and the abolition of tax breaks to yield $1.8 billion in 1997.
But much of the money will go to finance a huge armaments programme in the next five years to deter territorial ambitions by neighbouring Turkey on Greek islands in the Aegean Sea.
"Trillions of drachmas (billions of dollars) will be invested in the next five years to safeguard our national sovereignty," Defence Minister Akis Tsohatzopoulos said. "We have no choice."
Defence ministry officials told Reuters the bill could reach $10 billion and will include F-16 fighters, missiles, attack helicopters and other military equipment.
Greece spends 4.6 percent of its GDP on defence, more than most other NATO members. The decision for the arms purchase was expected by the end of the year.
Simitis said during his pre-election campaign that the arms bill could be partly financed through foreign borrowing.
